newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission to be the focus of late 1996 work.
newsitem.headline: Commission to be the focus of late 1996 work.

text.p: The European Commission is once again the likely focus of attention during the remainder of 1996, with a pile of draft environment texts awaiting adoption.
Many of these have completed their travels through inter-service discussions within the Commission and now await the final stage through cabinet-level negotiations and the Commission itself.
The most that can be said about their timings for now is that they should make it to adoption before the end of the year, said a source close to European Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard.
Such caution comes after last year, when the Commissioner and her cohorts found themselves overwhelmed by all the texts due for adoption, with many ending up having to wait.
One file approaching the top of the pile is the planned communication on methane, for which inter-service consultations were completed before the summer.
The proposal should come before the Commission "some time within the next eight weeks", the source said.

Another item on the to do list is the review of Directive 90/220 on the deliberate release of genetically modified organisms to the environment. This has been brought to the fore with the recent problems surrounding EU approval of a maize strain marketed by Swiss company Ciba-Geigy AG.

"We have a report prepared on the functioning of the directive which has been through inter-service consultation. It's a critical report and will probably point to the need to revise the directive in 1997," the source said, adding that most problems related to the time taken to process requests.
A proposal to extend to strategic planning decisions the requirement for environmental impact assessments, so-called strategic EIAs, is also on the way.
"Discussions at inter-service have increased the consensus on this proposal so we stand a fair chance of getting this passed through," the source said.

The fate of four proposals related to air pollution -- namely for directives on the reduction of sulphur in liquid fuels, on reduction of volatile organic compounds (solvents) emissions, the second stage of limiting emissions of volatile organic compounds in the vehicle fuel supply chain (VOC II), and the acidification strategy -- all hang together.
"We have not yet taken a decision on how to go forward with these. They are not one hundred percent related but they are related to a certain extent," the source said.
"With VOC stage II for example, things are already going ahead on this in several member states," the source said.

As far as the acidification strategy is concerned, part of the intention was to help underpin arguments for the sulphur in liquid fuels draft directive, which was rebuffed last time it was presented for Commission scrutiny. A decision on the timing of the directive versus that of the strategy is still awaited.
Whether or not the Commission will propose an EU negotiating mandate for next year's third U.N. conference of the parties (COP III) on climate change remains to a large part in member states' hands.

"It's a controversial question for which we are not really sure where member states are. What we are talking about is a mandate for COP III in Japan or a Council resolution. There will be discussions on this issue, probably at both Councils this year. Whether we go ahead with a mandate will depend on the outcome of these," the source said.

"Whether it's a mandate for Community negotiators or a Council resolution is open to debate. There are pros and cons for each. If a Community mandate is too rigid then it may make the Community's tactics too inflexible. On the other hand, we are getting close to a situation where we will have to talk about specific targets (for reductions in carbon dioxide emissions after 2000)," the source added.
Two proposals for directives related to aircraft, one on noise the other on engine emissions of nitorus oxide, are also on the books for Commission adoption before the year-end.

The planned communication on a framework for environmental liability is scheduled for a first debate in Commission within the next two months, as is the proposal related to implementation of EU environmental law.
"Both them require broad discussions within the Commission and maybe first an orientation debate to see what the Commission says," the source said.
A framework agreement governing member state environmental levies and taxes is less well-advanced with some work remaining to be done at inter-service level.
Questions surrounding the patchy implementation and operation of Directive 90/313/EEC, on access to environmental information, remain lower on the list of priorities.
"I am not sure that we will go ahead with this because it's been taken up by others in institutional negotiations," the source said.
A proposal on future EU policy to combat noise pollution, possibly a legislative instrument or a green paper, is also looming, possibly for September.

The planned proposal for a framework directive on water remains a matter for discussions with the European Parliament, even before the Commission has adopted its draft proposal, with the assembly yet to decide on whether it will push for an action programme or a framework directive. A programme would allow parliament greater influence in drawing up the legislation but could compromise the eventual text, which would be less legally robust than a directive.
"We still hope that towards the end of the year we will be able to put forward our framework directive," the source said.
Another item for the Commission is the question of how to proceed with a framework governing voluntary environmental agreements between government and industry.

"These kinds of agreements should be seen as a supplement to the legislation. Since they are already happening, it would be a good idea to have a framework on how they should work. What we are trying to do is to explain what are the problems and advantages with these kinds of agreements.
"At the Community level, can you identify a limited number of actors with whom to negotiate?," the source said.
Finally, the Commission has promised to look at the way the eco-label programme, as defined by Council Regulation 880/92, has operated.

"It's not to abolish the system but to try to improve it so that it's got more meaning in real life. There are a number of different aspects with it which will be addressed in the review," the source said.
Moving to the Council of Ministers, Ireland has a chance to tackle some new files during the remaining four months of its presidency. Councils are scheduled for October 15/16 and December 9/10.
"Our main common position hopes would be with the fifth framework action programme review and the GMOs Directive 90/219," a presidency diplomat told Reuters.
"Among the other important things would be the drinking water directive COM(94)612 and the auto/oil proposals, we hope to have substantial orientation debates on both of those," the diplomat said.
Ministers will also discuss the follow-up to June's conference on climate change and prepare the EU position for protocol negotiations.

Other international get-togethers requiring Council attention include preparations for the conference on bio-diversity, for the eighth meeting of the parties to the Montreal protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer and the fifth session of the Commission on sustainable development.
Ministers will also have a crack at the Commission's communication on waste strategy, COM(96)399, though delays in the adoption of this have also inhibited Ireland's chances of substanital progress.

It remains to be seen what action environment ministers take on proposal COM(95)737 for a Council regulation amending Council Regulation (EEC) No 3254/91 prohibiting the use of leghold traps in the Community and on the import of pelts of animals which are caught using methods defined as inhumane by international rules.
Their decision, to be based on the outcome of talks between the Commission and Russia, Canada and the United States, will be a tricky one.

Another item to consider will be proposal COM(95)143 for a Council regulation establishing common rules and procedures to apply to the shipments to certain non-OECD countries of certain types of waste.
